newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt-Israel gas "peace pipeline" slow going.
newsitem.headline: Egypt-Israel gas "peace pipeline" slow going.

text.p: A "peace pipeline" project to export Egyptian gas to Israel is at a standstill as Israel decides on purchase and transport issues, and one official said politics was one factor in delays.

"The ball is in their (the Israeli) court," said Mark Klingseisen, Amoco business development director, on Tuesday. "They do not have a gas or organisational infrastructure since it is a new fuel for them."
One Egyptian oil industry source close to the project said: "Political conditions made it stop."
Another said that Egypt has simply shifted its focus to the more attractive option of exporting natural gas to Turkey.
The pipeline, known as the "peace pipeline" because of the political symbolism, has been under discussion for years.

Talks on sales of Egyptian gas to Israel were between Israel Electric Corp (IEC), which is expected to consume 70 percent of future Israeli demand for natural gas, and Amoco and Agip, the foreign companies developing the gas fields off the Nile Delta.

The commercial aspect of the deal is being handled by the private companies. Both countries will have to sanction any deal. The two countries have a peace treaty but also differences over the Middle East peace process.
Oil Minister Hamdi el-Banbi had told a news conference in April that Egypt was not giving the project high priority.
Asked if he thought the current freeze in the Middle East peace process was hindering movement in the project, Klingseisen said: "There is still a political peace process. It is still delicate."
"There's gas in Egypt and a market in Jordan and Israel. It (the peace process) is no more a factor than it's ever been, to my knowledge it hasn't impeded the progress," he said.

"The issue is does the Israeli government want to set up a purchaser or should they allow the IEC to negotiate on their own. There are a lot of internal struggles on which way to go for the short and long term."
The proposed project involved the export of about two to four billion cubic metres of Egyptian gas a year to Israel.

"The Israeli Infrastructure Ministry is contemplating whether to allow the IEC to negotiate for their volumes of gas on their own, and then more than likely the government would tender for a company that would be responsible for buying and selling gas for the rest of the market, residential and commercial.

"Other options are to tender for a company and let it do all the buying and selling. They have to create a company and want it to be non-governmental as well as have foreign interests involved," Klingseisen said.
An outstanding issue is whether the pipeline route should be offshore or onshore and concerns of the onshore pipeline include cost and procuring land rights from owners, he said.
"When they assess the situation I believe it will take some time to get everyone's approval. It may have to go through some congested heavy populated areas," he said.
